reviviscence: The act of reviving, or the state of being revived; renewal of life. In this age we have a sort of reviviscence, not, I fear, of the power, but of a taste for the power, of the early times. Coleridge.
regreet: To greet again; to resalute; to return a salutation to; to greet. Shak. | A return or exchange of salutation.
restem: 1. To force back against the current; as, to restem their backward course. Shak. 2. To stem, or as, to restem a current.
reprimer: A machine or implement for applying fresh primers to spent cartridge shells, so that the shells be used again.
rectal: Of or pertaining to the rectum; in the region of the rectum.
reentrant: Reëntering; pointing or directed inwardds; as, a re angle.
renege: To deny; to disown. (old) Shak. All Europe high (all sorts of rights reneged) Against the trith and thee unholy leagued. Sylvester. | 1. To deny. (old) Shak. 2. (Card Playing) To revoke.
refrigerative: Cooling; allaying heat. -- n. A refrigerant. Crazed brains should come under a refrigerative treatment. I. Taylor.
rebuild: To build again, as something which has been demolished; to construct anew; as, to rebuild a house, a wall, a wharf, or a city.
retinalite: A translucent variety of serpentine, of a honey yellow or greenish yellow color, having a waxy resinlike luster.
reichstag: The Diet, or House of Representatives, of the German empire, which is composed of members elected for a term of three years by the direct vote of the people. See Bundesrath.
restrain: 1. To draw back again; to hold back from acting, proceeding, or advancing, either by physical or moral force, or by any interposing obstacle; to repress or suppress; to keep down; to curb. repsilver: Money anciently paid by servile tenants to their lord, in lieu of the customary service of reaping his corn or grain.
residentiaryship: The office or condition of a residentiary.
recency: The state or quality of being recent; newness; new state; late origin; lateness in time; freshness; as, the recency of a transaction, of a wound, etc.
reconcile: 1. To cause to be friendly again; to conciliate anew; to restore to friendship; to bring back to harmony; to cause to be no longer at variance; as, to reconcile persons who have quarreled. reillumine: To illumine again or anew; to reillume.
retortion: 1. Act of retorting or throwing back; reflection or turning back. [Written also retorsion.] It was, however, necessary to possess some single term expressive of this intellectual retortion. Sir W. Hamilton. 2. (Law) Retaliation. Wharton.
resistless: 1. Having no power to resist; making no opposition. [Obs. or R.] Spenser. 2. Incapable of being resisted; irresistible. Masters' commands come with a power resistless To such as owe them absolute subjection. Milton. -- Re*sist"less*ly, adv. -- Re*sist"less*ness, n.
redintegration: 1. Restoration to a whole or sound state; renewal; renovation. Dr. H. More. 2. (Chem.) Restoration of a mixed body or matter to its former nature and state. [Achaic.] Coxe. 3. redif: A reserve force in the Turkish army, or a soldier of the reserve. See Army organization, above.

revoluble: Capable of revolving; rotatory; revolving. (old) Us, then, to whom the thrice three year Hath filled his revoluble orb since our arrival here, I blame not. Chapman.
remissible: Capable of being remitted or forgiven. Feltham.
reng: 1. A rank; a row. (old) "In two renges fair." Chaucer. 2. A rung or round of a ladder. (old) Chaucer.
recriminate: To return one charge or accusation with another; to chargeback fault or crime upon an accuser. It is not my business to recriminate, hoping sufficiently toBp. Stillingfleet.
redoubtable: Formidable; dread; terrible to foes; as, a redoubtable hero; hence, valiant; -- often in contempt or burlesque. [Written also redoutable.]
reconjoin: To join or conjoin anew. Boyle.
receivability: The quality of being receivable; receivableness.
rentier: One who has a fixed income, as from lands, stocks, or the like.
remise: To send, give, or grant back; torelease a claim to; to resign or surrender by deed; to return. Blackstone. | A giving or granting back; surrender; return; release, as of a claim.
rescribe: 1. To write back; to write in reply. Ayliffe. 2. To write over again. Howell.
resorption: The act of resorbing; also, the act of absorbing again; reabsorption.
recurvate: To bend or curve back; to recurve. Pennant.
reactionary: Being, causing, or favoring reaction; as, reactionary movements. | One who favors reaction, or seeks to undo political progress or revolution.
refortification: A fortifying anew, or a second time. Mitford.
reciprocally: 1. In a reciprocal manner; so that each affects the other, and is equally affected by it; interchangeably; mutually. These two particles to reciprocally affect each other with the same force. Bentley. 2. (Math.) In the manner of reciprocals. Reciprocally proportional (Arith.

retention: 1. The act of retaining, or the state of being ratined. 2. The power of retaining; retentiveness. No woman's heart So big, to hold so much; they lack retention. Shak. 3. renewable: Capable of being renewed; as, a lease renewable at pleasure. Swift.
reformed: 1. Corrected; amended; restored to purity or excellence; said, specifically, of the whole body of Protestant churches originating in the Reformation. reimport: To import again; to import what has been exported; to bring back. Young.
repentant: 1. Penitent; sorry for sin. Chaucer. Thus they, in lowliest plight, repentant stood. Millton. 2. Expressing or showing sorrow for sin; as, repentant tears; repentant ashes. | One who repents, especially one who repents of sin; a penitent.
reticulated: 1. Resembling network; having the form or appearance of a net; netted; as, a reticulated structure. 2. Having veins, fibers, or lines crossing like the threads or fibers of a network; as, a reticulate leaf; a reticulated surface; a reticulated wing of an insect.
remiped: Having feet or legs that are used as oars; -- said of certain crustaceans and insects. | (a) An animal having limbs like oars, especially one of certain crustaceans. (b) One of a group of aquatic beetles having tarsi adapted for swimming. See Water beetle.
refuse: 1. To deny, as a request, demand, invitation, or command; to decline to do or grant. That never yet refused your hest. Chaucer. 2. (Mil.) redan: 1. (Fort.) A work having two parapets whose faces unite so as to form a salient angle toward the enemy. 2. A step or vertical offset in a wall on uneven ground, to keep the parts level.
reefer: 1. (Naut.) One who reefs; -- a name often given to midshipmen. Marryat. 2. A close-fitting lacket or short coat of thick cloth.
relativeness: The state of being relative, or having relation; relativity.
reflectent: 1. Bending or flying back; reflected. "The ray descendent, and the ray reflectent flying with so great a speed." Sir K. Digby. 2. Reflecting; as, a reflectent body. Sir K. Digby.
remissory: Serving or tending to remit, or to secure remission; remissive. "A sacrifice expiatory or remissory." Latimer.
renate: Born again; regenerate; renewed. (old) Beau & Fl.

revert: 1. To turn back, or to the contrary; to reverse. Till happy chance revert the cruel scence. Prior. The tumbling stream . . . Reverted, plays in undulating flow. Thomson. 2. remorseful: 1. Full of remorse. The full tide of remorseful passion had abated. Sir W. Scott. 2. Compassionate; feeling tenderly. (old) Shak. 3. Exciting pity; pitiable. (old) Chapman. -- Re*morse"ful*ly, adv. -- Re*morse"ful*ness, n.
respecter: One who respects. A respecter of persons, one who regards or judges with partiality. Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons. Acts x. 34.

revocable: Capable of being revoked; as, a revocable edict or grant; a revocable covenant. -- Rev"o*ca*ble*ness, n. -- Rev"o*ca*bly, adv.
repellency: The principle of repulsion; the quality or capacity of repelling; repulsion.
requisitor: One who makes reqisition; esp., one authorized by a requisition to investigate facts.
recelebrate: To celebrate again, or anew. -- Re*cel`e*bra"tion, n.
remastication: The act of masticating or chewing again or repeatedly.

redigest: To digest, or reduce to form, a second time. Kent.
reactance: The influence of a coil of wire upon an alternating current passing through it, tending to choke or diminish the current, or the similar influence of a condenser; inductive resistance. Reactance is measured in ohms.
reefband: A piece of canvas sewed across a sail to strengthen it in the part where the eyelet holes for reefing are made. Totten.
resistibility: 1. The quality of being resistible; resistibleness. 2. The quality of being resistant; resitstance. The name "body" being the complex idea of extension and resistibility together in the same subject. Locke.
relive: To recall to life; to revive. (old)
reremouse: The leather-winged bat (Vespertilio murinus). [Written also reermouse.]

revolting: Causing abhorrence mixed with disgust; exciting extreme repugnance; loathsome; as, revolting cruelty. -- Re*volt"ing*ly, adv.
reentrance: The act entereing again; re Hooker.
reconvey: 1. To convey back or to the former place; as, to reconvey goods. 2. To transfer back to a former owner; as, to reconvey an estate.
redstart: (a) A small, handsome European singing bird (Ruticilla phoenicurus), allied to the nightingale; -- called also redtail, brantail, fireflirt, firetail. The black redstart is P.tithys. repairer: One who, or that which, repairs, restores, or makes amends.
retaliatory: Tending to, or involving, retaliation; retaliative; as retaliatory measures.
redhanded: Having hands red with blood; in the very act, as if with red or bloody hands; -- said of a person taken in the act of homicide; hence, fresh from the commission of crime; as, he was taken red-hand or red-handed.
retraxit: The withdrawing, or open renunciation, of a suit in court by the plaintiff, by which he forever lost his right of action. Blackstone.
remord: To excite to remorse; to rebuke. (old) Skelton. | To feel remorse. (old) Sir T. Elyot.
recapitulatory: Of the nature of a recapitulation; containing recapitulation.
resend: 1. To send again; as, to resend a message. 2. To send back; as, to resend a gift. (old) Shak. 3. (Telegraphy) To send on from an intermediate station by means of a repeater.
repugnant: Disposed to fight against; hostile; at war with; being at variance; contrary; inconsistent; refractory; disobedient; also, distasteful in a high degree; offensive; -- usually followed by to, rarely and less properly by with; as, all rudeness was repugnant to her nature. relict: A woman whose husband is dead; a widow. Eli dying without issue, Jacob was obbliged by law to marry his relict, and so to raise up seed to his brother Eli. South.
rememoration: A recalling by the faculty of memory; remembrance. [Obs. & R.] Bp. Montagu.
reintegrate: To renew with regard to any state or quality; to restore; to bring again together into a whole, as the parts off anything; to reas, to reintegrate a nation. Bacon.
remontant: Rising again; -- applied to a class of roses which bloom more than once in a season; the hybrid perpetual roses, of which the Jacqueminot is a well-known example.
reedify: To edify anew; to build again after destruction. Milton.
recompense: 1. To render an equivalent to, for service, loss, etc.; to requite; to remunerate; to compensate. He can not recompense me better. Shak. 2. To return an equivalent for; to give compensation for; | To give recompense; to make amends or requital. (old)
reduce: 1. To bring or lead back to any former place or condition. (old) And to his brother's house reduced his wife. Chapman. To bring to any inferior state, with respect to rank, size, quantity, quality, value, etc.; to diminish; to lower;
regressive: 1. Passing back; returning. 2. Characterized by retrogression; retrogressive. Regressive metamorphism. (a) (Biol.) See Retrogression. (b) (Physiol.) See Katabolism.

resinic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, resin; as, the resinic acids.
refurnishment: The act of refurnishing, or state of being refurnished. The refurnishment was in a style richer than before. L. Wallace.

religieux: A person bound by monastic vows; a nun; a monk.

rewin: To win again, or win back. The Palatinate was not worth the rewinning. Fuller.
redeemableness: The quality or state of being redeemable; redeemability.
reinterrogate: To interrogate again; to question repeatedly. Cotgrave.
remind: To put (one) in mind of something; to bring to the remembrance of; to bring to the notice or consideration of (a person). When age itself, which will not be defied, shall begin to arrest, seize, and remind us of our mortality. South.
regnal: Of or pertaining to the reign of a monarch; as, regnal years.
reconciliatory: Serving or tending to reconcile. Bp. Hall.
rebucous: Rebuking. (old) She gave unto him many rebucous words. Fabyan.

replenish: 1. To fill again after having been diminished or emptied; to stock anew; hence, to fill completely; to cause to abound. Multiply and replenish the earth. Gen. i. 28. | To recover former fullness. (old) The humors will not replenish so soon. Bacon.
repullulation: The act of budding again; the state of having budded again.
revocation: 1. The act of calling back, or the state of being recalled; recall. One that saw the people bent for the revocation of Calvin, gave him notice of their affection. Hooker. 2. The act by which one, having the right, annuls an act done, a power or authority given, or a license, gift, or benefit conferred; repeal; reversal;
remissful: Inclined to remit punishment; lenient; clement. Drayton.
requicken: To quicken anew; to reanimate; to give new life to. Shak.
remanet: A case for trial which can not be tried during the term; a postponed case. [Eng.]
reiter: A German cavalry soldier of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.
recuse: To refuse or reject, as a judge; to challenge that the judge shall not try the cause. (old) Sir K. Digby.
rejoin: 1. To join again; to unite after separation. 2. To come, or go, again into the presence of; to join the company of again. Meet and rejoin me, in the pensive grot. Pope. 3. To state in reply; | 1. To answer to a reply. 2. (Law) To answer, as the defendant to the plaintiff's replication.
reptantia: A divisiom of gastropods; the Pectinibranchiata.
recusation: 1. Refusal. (old) 2. (Old Law) The act of refusing a judge or challenging that he shall not try the cause, on account of his supposed partiality. Blackstone.
release: To lease again; to grant a new lease of; to let back. | 1. To let loose again; to set free from restraint, confinement, or servitude; to give liberty to, or to set at liberty; to let go. Now at that feast he released unto them one prisoner, whomsoever…
redundancy: 1. The quality or state of being redundant; superfluity; superabundance; excess. 2. That which is redundant or in excess; anything superfluous or superabundant. Labor . . . throws off redundacies. Addison. 3. (Law) Surplusage inserted in a pleading which may be rejected by the court without impairing the validity of what remains.
reimbursable: Capable of being repaid; repayable. A loan has been made of two millions of dollars, reimbursable in ten years. A. Hamilton.
responsory: Containing or making answer; answering. Johnson. | 1. (Eccl.) (a) The answer of the people to the priest in alternate speaking, in church service. (b) A versicle sung in answer to the priest, or as a refrain. Which, if should repeat again, would turn…
reefing: The process of taking in a reef. Reefing bowsprit, a bowsprit so rigged that it can easily be run in or shortened by sliding inboard, as in cutters.
resistance: 1. The act of resisting; opposition, passive or active. When King Demetrius saw that . . . no resistance was made against him, he sent away all his forces. 1. Macc. xi. 38. 2. (Physics) The quality of not yielding to force or external pressure; that power of a body which acts in opposition to the impulse or pressure of another, or which prevents the effect of another power;
reave: To take away by violence or by stealth; to snatch away; to rob; to despoil; to bereave. (old). "To reave his life." Spenser. He golden apples raft of the dragon. Chaucer. By privy stratagem my life at home. Chapman. To reave the orphan of his patrimony. Shak. The heaven caught and reft him of his tongue. Tennyson.
repartotion: Another, or an additional, separation into parts.
revince: To overcome; to refute, as error. (old) Foxe.
redress: 1. To put in order again; to set right; to emend; to revise. The common profit could she redress. Chaucer. In yonder spring of roses intermixed With myrtle, find what to redress till noon. Milton. | 1. The act of redressing; a making right; reformation; correction; amendment. Reformation of evil laws is commendable, but for us the more necessary is a speedy redress of ourselves. Hooker. 2.
respondent: Disposed or expected to respond; answering; according; corresponding. Wealth respondent to payment and contributions. Bacon. | One who responds. It corresponds in general to defendant. Specifically: (a) (Law) One who answers in certain suits or proceedings, generally those which are not according to the course of the common…
rechauffe: A dish of food that has been warmed again, hence, fig., something made up from old material; a rehash. It is merely a réchauffé of ancient philosophies. F. W. H. Myers.
refrigerator: That which refrigerates or makes cold; that which keeps cool. Specifically: (a) A box or room for keeping food or other articles cool, usually by means of ice. (b) An apparatus for rapidly cooling heated liquids or vapors, connected with a still, etc.
retiracy: Retirement; -- mostly used in a jocose or burlesque way. [U.S.] Bartlett. What one of our great men used to call dignified retiracy. C. A. Bristed.
regrant: To grant back; to grant again or anew. Ayliffe. | 1. The act of granting back to a former proprietor. 2. A renewed of a grant; as, the regrant of a monopoly.
repealable: Capable of being repealed. -- Re*peal"a*ble*ness, n. Syn. -- Revocable; abrogable; voidable; reversible.
rejourn: To adjourn; to put off. (old) Shak.
retractile: CApable of retraction; capable of being drawn back or up; as, the claws of a cat are retractile.
realm: 1. A royal jurisdiction or domain; a region which is under the dominion of a king; a kingdom. The absolute master of realms on which the sun perpetually alone. Motley. 2. Hence, in general, province; region; country; domain; department; division; as, the realm of fancy.
report: 1. To refer. (old) Baldwin, his son, . . . succeeded his father; so like unto him that we report the reader to the character of King Almeric, and will spare the repeating his description. Fuller. 2. | 1. To make a report, or response, in respect of a matter inquired of, a duty enjoined, or information expected; as, the committee will report at twelve o'clock. 2.
redshank: 1. (Zoöl.) (a) A common Old World limicoline bird (Totanus calidris), having the legs and feet pale red. The spotted redshank (T. fuscus) is larger, and has orange-red legs. Called also redshanks, redleg, and clee. (b) The fieldfare. 2. A bare-legged person; -- a contemptuous appellation formerly given to the Scotch Highlanders, in allusion to their bare legs. Spenser.
repress: 1. To press back or down effectually; to crush down or out; to quell; to subdue; to supress; as, to repress sedition or rebellion; to repress the first risings of discontent. 2. Hence, to check; to restrain; to keep back. Desire of wine and all delicious drinks, . . . Thou couldst repress. Milton. Syn. -- To crush; overpower; subdue; suppress; restrain; quell; curb; check.
regard: 1. To keep in view; to behold; to look at; to view; to gaze upon. Your niece regards me with an eye of favor. Shak. 2. Hence, to look or front toward; to face. (old) It is peninsula which regardeth… | To look attentively; to consider; to notice. (old) Shak.
readdress: To address a second time; -- often used reflexively. He readdressed himself to her. Boyle.
repose: 1. To cause to stop or to rest after motion; hence, to deposit; to lay down; to lodge; to reposit. (old) But these thy fortunes let us straight repose In this divine cave's bosom. Chapman. | 1. To lie at rest; to rest. Within a thicket I reposed. Chapman. 2. Figuratively, to remain or abide restfully without anxiety or alarms. It is upon these that the soul may repose. I. Taylor. 3.
retroflexion: The act of reflexing; the state of being retroflexed. Cf. Retroversion.
resistant: Making resistance; resisting. -- n. One who, or that which, resists. Bp. Pearson.
retainer: 1. One who, or that which, retains. 2. One who is retained or kept in service; an attendant; an adherent; a hanger-on. 3. Hence, a servant, not a domestic, but occasionally attending and wearing his master's livery. Cowell. 4. (Law) (a) The act of a client by which he engages a lawyer or counselor to manage his cause.
regular: 1. Conformed to a rule; agreeable to an established rule, law, principle, or type, or to established customary forms; normal; symmetrical; as, a regular verse in poetry; a regular piece of music; | 1. (R. C. Ch.) A member of any religious order or community who has taken the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, and who has been solemnly recognized by the church. Bp. Fitzpatrick. 2.
recentness: Quality or state of being recent.
refracted: 1. (Bot. & Zoöl.) Bent backward angularly, as if half-broken; as, a refracted stem or leaf. 2. Turned from a direct course by refraction; as, refracted rays of light.
republish: To publish anew; specifically, to publish in one country (a work first published in another); also, to revive (a will) by re Subsecquent to the purchase or contract, the devisor republished his will. Blackstone.
redmouth: Any one of several species of marine food fishes of the genus Diabasis, or Hæmulon, of the Southern United States, having the inside of the mouth bright red. Called also flannelmouth, and grunt.
recrudesce: To be in a state of recrudescence; esp., to come into renewed freshness, vigor, or activity; to revive. The general influence . . . which is liable every now and then to recrudesce in his absence. Edmund Gurney.
rezdechaussee: The ground story of a building, either on a level with the street or raised slightly above it; -- said esp. of buildings on the continent of Europe. Tier above tier of neat apartments rise over the little shops which form the rez-de-chaussée. The Century.
reticle: 1. A small net. 2. A reticule. See Reticule,2.
redfin: A small North American dace (Minnilus cornutus, or Notropis megalops). The male, in the breeding season, has bright red fins. Called also red dace, and shiner. Applied also to Notropis ardens, of the Mississippi valley.
rereiterate: To reiterate many times. "My re-reiterated wish." Tennyson.
relational: 1. Having relation or kindred; related. We might be tempted to take these two nations for relational stems. Tooke. 2. Indicating or specifying some relation. Relational words, as prepositions, auxiliaries, etc. R. Morris.
regularia: A division of Echini which includes the circular, or regular, sea urchins.
regenesis: New birth; renewal. A continued regenesis of dissenting sects. H. Spenser.
reaper: 1. One who reaps. The sun-burned reapers wiping their foreheads. Macaulay. 2. A reaping machine.
refrigerant: Cooling; allaying heat or fever. Bacon. | That which makes to be cool or cold; specifically, a medicine or an application for allaying fever, or the symptoms of fever; -- used also figuratively. Holland. "A refrigerant to passion." Blair.
remove: 1. To move away from the position occupied; to cause to change place; to displace; as, to remove a building. Thou shalt not remove thy neighbor's landmark. Deut. xix. 14. | To change place in any manner, or to make a change in place; to move or go from one residence, position, or place to another. Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane, I can not taint with fear. Shak.
resolve: 1. To separate the component parts of; to reduce to the constituent elements; -- said of compound substances; hence, sometimes, to melt, or dissolve. O, that this too too solid flesh would melt,… | 1. To be separated into its component parts or distinct principles; to undergo resolution. 2. To melt; to dissolve; to become fluid. When the blood stagnates in any part, it first coagulates, then…
reconcilable: Capable of being reconciled; as, reconcilable adversaries; an act reconciable with previous acts. The different accounts of the numbers of ships are reconcilable. Arbuthnot. -- Rec"on*ci`la*ble*ness, n. -- Rec"on*ci`la*bly, adv.
recessed: 1. Having a recess or recesses; as, a recessed arch or wall. 2. Withdrawn; secluded. "Comfortably recessed from curious impertinents." Miss Edgeworth. Recessed arch (Arch.), one of a series of arches constructed one within another so as to correspond with splayed jambs of a doorway, or the like.
redgum: 1. (Med.) An eruption of red pimples upon the face, neck, and arms, in early infancy; tooth rash; strophulus. Good. 2. A name of rust on grain. See Rust.
resorcin: A colorless crystalline substance of the phenol series, obtained by melting certain resins, as galbanum, asafetida, etc., with caustic potash. It is also produced artificially and used in making certain dyestuffs, as phthaleïn, fluoresceïn, and eosin.
repletion: 1. The state of being replete; superabundant fullness. The tree had too much repletion, and was oppressed with its own sap. Bacon. Replecioun [overeating] ne made her never sick. Chaucer. 2. (Med.) Fullness of blood; plethora.
reaction: 1. Any action in resisting other action or force; counter tendency; movement in a contrary direction; reverse action. 2. (Chem.) retentor: A muscle which serves to retain an organ or part in place, esp. when retracted. See Illust. of Phylactolemata.
retardation: 1. The act of retarding; hindrance; the act of delaying; as, the retardation of the motion of a ship; -- opposed to Ant: acceleration. The retardations of our fluent motion. De Quinsey. 2. That which retards; an obstacle; an obstruction. Hills, sloughs, and other terrestrial retardations. Sir W. Scott. 3.
reassign: To assign back or again; to transfer back what has been assigned.
renitent: 1. Resisting pressure or the effect of it; acting against impluse by elastic force. "[Muscles] soft and yet renitent." Ray. 2. Persistently opposed.
resupination: The state of luing on the back; the state of being resupinate, or reversed. Our Vitruvius calleth this affection in the eye a resupination of the figure. Sir H. Wotton.
repossession: The act or the state of possessing again.
reverberate: 1. Reverberant. (old) "The reverberate hills." Shak. 2. Driven back, as sound; reflected. (old) Drayton. | 1. To return or send back; to repel or drive back; to echo, as sound; to reflect, as light, as light or heat. Who, like an arch, reverberates The voice again. Shak. 2. To send or force back;
rescussor: One who makes an unlawful rescue; a rescuer. Burril.
reechy: Smoky; reeky; hence, begrimed with dirt. (old)
retroflexed: Reflexed; bent or turned abruptly backward.
retinic: Of or pertaining to resin; derived from resin; specifically, designating an acid found in certain fossil resins and hydrocarbons.
reticulose: Forming a network; characterized by a reticulated sructure. Reticulose rhizopod (Zoöl.), a rhizopod in which the pseudopodia blend together and form irregular meshes.
repudiation: The act of repudiating, or the state of being repuddiated; as, the repudiation of a doctrine, a wife, a debt, etc. | One who favors repudiation, especially of a public debt.
reglement: Regulation. (old) The reformation and reglement of usuary. Bacon.
rearrange: To arrange again; to arrange in a different way.
representative: 1. Fitted to represent; exhibiting a similitude. 2. Bearing the character or power of another; acting for another or others; as, a council representative of the people. Swift. 3. | 1. One who, or that which, represents (anything); that which exhibits a likeness or similitude. A statute of Rumor, whispering an idiot in the ear, who was the representative of Credulity. Addison.
refrigeratory: That which refrigerates or cools. Specifically: (a) In distillation, a vessel filled with cold water, surrounding the worm, the vapor in which is thereby condensed. (b) The chamber, or tank, in which ice is formed, in an ice machine.
renable: Reasonable; also, loquacious. (old) "Most renable of tongue." Piers Plowman. -- Ren"a*bly, adv. (old) Chaucer.
reanswer: To answer in return; to repay; to compensate; to make amends for. Which in weight to reanswer, his pettiness would bow under. Shak.
resentful: Inclined to resent; easily provoked to anger; irritable. -- Re*sent"ful*ly, adv.
reservist: A member of a reserve force of soldiers or militia. [Eng.]
reforestization: The act or process of reforestizing.
rebozo: A kind of mantilla worn by women over the head and shoulders, and sometimes over part of the face. [Mexico & Sp. Amer.]
reinette: A name given to many different kinds of apples, mostly of French origin.
reship: To ship again; to put on board of a vessel a second time; to send on a second voyage; as, to reship bonded merchandise. | To engage one's self again for service on board of a vessel after having been discharged.
reconvert: A person who has been reconverted. Gladstone.
recreate: To give fresh life to; to reanimate; to revive; especially, to refresh after wearying toil or anxiety; to relieve; to cheer; to divert; to amuse; to gratify. Painters, when they work on white… | To take recreation. L. Addison.
revolt: 1. To turn away; to abandon or reject something; specifically, to turn away, or shrink, with abhorrence. But this got by casting pearl to hogs, That bawl for freedom in their senseless mood, And… | 1. To cause to turn back; to roll or drive back; to put to flight. (old) Spenser. 2. To do violence to; to cause to turn away or shrink with abhorrence; to shock; as, to revolt the feelings.
redtail: (a) The red-tailed hawk. (b) The European redstart.
readjustment: A second adjustment; a new or different adjustment.
recaptor: One who recaptures; one who takes a prize which had been previously taken.
regularly: In a regular manner; in uniform order; methodically; in due order or time.
reenforce: To strengthen with new force, assistance, material, or support; as, to reënforce an argument; to reënforce a garment; especially, to strengthen with additional troops, as an army or a fort, or with… | Something which reënforces or strengthens. Specifically: (a) That part of a cannon near the breech which is thicker than the rest of the piece, so as better to resist the force of the exploding…
religionary: Relating to religion; pious; as, religionary professions. (old)
retroflex: Reflexed; bent or turned abruptly backward.
revolutionist: One engaged in effecting a change of government; a favorer of revolution. Burke.
recluseness: Quality or state of being recluse.
reach: 1. To extend; to stretch; to thrust out; to put forth, as a limb, a member, something held, or the like. Her tresses yellow, and long straughten, Unto her heeles down they raughten. Rom. of R. | 1. To stretch out the hand. Goddess humane, reach, then, and freely taste! Milton. 2. To strain after something; to make efforts. Reaching above our nature does no good. Dryden. 3.
reticent: Inclined to keep silent; reserved; uncommunicative.
repudiate: 1. To cast off; to disavow; to have nothing to do with; to renounce; to reject. Servitude is to be repudiated with greater care. Prynne. 2. To divorce, put away, or discard, as a wife, or a woman one has promised to marry. His separation from Terentis, whom he repudiated not long afterward. Bolingbroke. 3. To refuse to acknowledge or to pay; to disclaim;
refluency: The quality of being refluent; a flowing back.
refreyd: To chill; to cool. (old) Refreyded by sickness . . . or by cold drinks. Chaucer.
refuge: 1. Shelter or protection from danger or distress. Rocks, dens, and caves! But I in none of these Find place or refuge. Milton. We might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. Heb. vi. 18. 2. That which shelters or protects from danger, or from distress or calamity;
recommendatory: Serving to recommend; recommending; commendatory. Swift.
rescission: The act of rescinding, abrogating, annulling, or vacating; as, the rescission of a law, decree, or judgment.
retake: 1. To take or receive again. 2. To take from a captor; to recapture; as, to retake a ship or prisoners.
refection: Refreshment after hunger or fatique; a repast; a lunch. [His] feeble spirit inly felt refection. Spenser. Those Attic nights, and those refections of the gods. Curran.
recalcitrant: Kicking back; recalcitrating; hence, showing repugnance or opposition; refractory.
recur: 1. To come back; to return again or repeatedly; to come again to mind. When any word has been used to signify an idea, the old idea will recur in the mind when the word is heard. I. Watts. 2. To occur at a stated interval, or according to some regular rule; as, the fever will recur to-night. 3. To resort; to have recourse; to go for help.
respiration: 1. The act of respiring or breathing again, or catching one's breath. 2. Relief from toil or suffering: rest. (old) Till the day Appear of respiration to the just And vengeance to the wicked. Milton. 3. Interval; intermission. (old) Bp. Hall. 4. (Physiol.) The act of resping or breathing; the act of taking in and giving out air;
regorge: 1. To vomit up; to eject from the stomach; to throw back. Hayward. 2. To swallow again; to swallow back. Tides at highest mark regorge the flood. DRyden.
revile: To address or abuse with opprobrious and contemptuous language; to reproach. "And did not she herself revile me there" Shak. Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again. 1 Pet. ii. 23. Syn. | Reproach; reviling. (old) The gracious Judge, without revile, replied. Milton.
reimprisonment: The act of reimprisoning, or the state of being reimprisoned.
resupine: Lying on the back; supine; hence, careless. Sir K. Digby. He spake, and, downward swayed, fell resupine, With his huge neck aslant. Cowper.
reiterative: 1. (Gram.) A word expressing repeated or reiterated action. 2. A word formed from another, or used to form another, by repetition; as, dillydally.
restiform: Formed like a rope; -- applied especially to several ropelike bundles or masses of fibers on the dorsal side of the medulla oblongata.
retund: To blunt; to turn, as an edge; figuratively, to cause to be obtuse or dull; as, to retund confidence. Ray. Cudworth.
reversion: 1. The act of returning, or coming back; return. (old) After his reversion home, [he] was spoiled, also, of all that he brought with him. Foxe. 2. That which reverts or returns; residue. (old) The small reversion of this great navy which came home might be looked upon by religious eyes as relics. Fuller. 3.
reiterate: To repeat again and again; to say or do repeatedly; sometimes, to repeat. That with reiterated crimes he might Heap on himself damnation. Milton. You never spoke what did become you less Than this; which to reiterate were sin. Shak. Syn. -- To repeat; recapitulate; rehearse.
resell: To sell again; to sell what has been bought or sold; to retail.
recorder: 1. One who records; specifically, a person whose official duty it is to make a record of writings or transactions. 2. The title of the chief judical officer of some cities and boroughs; also, of the chief justice of an East Indian settlement. The Recorder of London is judge of the Lord Mayor's Court, and one of the commissioners of the Central Criminal Court. 3.
reversionary: Of or pertaining to a reversion; involving a reversion; to be enjoyed in succession, or after the termination of a particular estate; as, a reversionary interest or right. | That which is to be received in reversion.
repaint: To paint anew or again; as, to repaint a house; to repaint the ground of a picture.
regional: Of or pertaining to a particular region; sectional.
resurgence: The act of rising again; resurrection.
reafforest: To convert again into the forest, as a region of country.
regalia: 1. That which belongs to royalty. Specifically: (a) The rights and prerogatives of a king. (b) Royal estates and revenues. (c) Ensings, symbols, or paraphernalia of royalty. 2. | A kind of cigar of large size and superior quality; also, the size in which such cigars are classed.
repreve: To reprove. (old) "Repreve him of his vice." Chaucer.
redtop: A kind of grass (Agrostis vulgaris) highly valued in the United States for pasturage and hay for cattle; -- called also English grass, and in some localities herd's grass. See Illustration in Appendix. The tall redtop is Triodia seslerioides.
reason: 1. A thought or a consideration offered in support of a determination or an opinion; a just ground for a conclusion or an action; that which is offered or accepted as an explanation; | 1. To exercise the rational faculty; to deduce inferences from premises; to perform the process of deduction or of induction; to ratiocinate; to reach conclusions by a systematic comparison of facts.
repetitious: Repeating; containing repetition. [U.S.] Dr. T. Dwight.
recoiler: One who, or that which, recoils.
rejoindure: Act of joining again. (old) "Beguiles our lips of all rejoindure" (i.e., kisses). Shak.
receptivity: 1. The state or quality of being receptive. 2. (Kantian Philos.) The power or capacity of receiving impressions, as those of the external senses.
retrieve: 1. To find again; to recover; to regain; to restore from loss or injury; as, to retrieve one's character; to retrieve independence. With late repentance now they would retrieve The bodies they… | To discover and bring in game that has been killed or wounded; as, a dog naturally inclined to retrieve. Walsh.
region: 1. One of the grand districts or quarters into which any space or surface, as of the earth or the heavens, is conceived of as divided; hence, in general, a portion of space or territory of indefinite extent; country; province; district; tract. If thence he 'scappe, into whatever world, Or unknown region. Milton. 2. Tract, part, or space, lying about and including anything;
reinless: Not having, or not governed by, reins; hence, not checked or restrained.
rewardable: Worthy of reward. -- Re*ward"a*ble*ness, n. -- Re*ward"a*bly, adv.
remonstrant: Inclined or tending to remonstrate; expostulatory; urging reasons in opposition to something. | One who remonstrates; specifically (Eccl. retreatful: Furnishing or serving as a retreat. "Our retreatful flood." Chapman.
reentering: The process of applying additional colors, by applications of printing blocks, to patterns already partly colored.
reverence: 1. Profound respect and esteem mingled with fear and affection, as for a holy being or place; the disposition to revere; veneration. If thou be poor, farewell thy reverence. Chaucer. | To regard or treat with reverence; to regard with respect and affection mingled with fear; to venerate. Let . . . the wife see that she reverence her husband. Eph. v. 33.
reacher: 1. One who reaches. 2. An exaggeration. (old) Fuller.
readjuster: One who, or that which, readjusts; in some of the States of the United States, one who advocates a refunding, and sometimes a partial repudiation, of the State debt without the consent of the State's creditors.
reconsolidation: The act or process of reconsolidating; the state of being reconsolidated.
recurrency: The act of recurring, or state of being recurrent; return; resort; recourse. I shall insensibly go on from a rare to a frequent recurrence to the dangerous preparations. I. Taylor.
respectively: 1. As relating to each; particularly; as each belongs to each; as each refers to each in order; as, let each man respectively perform his duty. The impressions from the objects or the senses do mingle respectively every one with its kind. Bacon. 2. Relatively; not absolutely. (old) Sir W. Raleigh. 3. Partially; with respect to private views. (old) 4. With respect; regardfully.
reversibility: The quality of being reversible. Tyndall.
regelate: To freeze together again; to undergo regelation, as ice.
repack: To pack a second time or anew; as, to repack beef; to repack a trunk.
regularize: To cause to become regular; to regulate.
reem: The Hebrew name of a horned wild animal, probably the Urus. Note: In King James's Version it is called unicorn; in the Revised Version,wild ox. Job xxxix. 9. | To open (the seams of a vessel's planking) for the purpose of calking them. Reeming iron (Naut.), an iron chisel for reeming the seams of planks in calking ships.
revilement: The act of reviling; also, contemptuous language; reproach; abuse. Spenser.
remblai: Earth or materials made into a bank after having been excavated.
retry: To try (esp. judicially) a second time; as, to retry a case; to retry an accused person.
reverential: Proceeding from, or expressing, reverence; having a reverent quality; reverent; as, reverential fear or awe. "A reverential esteem of things sacred." South.
receipt: 1. The act of receiving; reception. "At the receipt of your letter." Shak. 2. Reception, as an act of hospitality. (old) Thy kind receipt of me. Chapman. 3. reflectingly: With reflection; also, with censure; reproachfully. Swift.
relish: 1. To taste or eat with pleasure; to like the flavor of; to partake of with gratification; hence, to enjoy; to be pleased with or gratified by; to experience pleasure from; as, to relish food. | To have a pleasing or appetizing taste; to give gratification; to have a flavor. Had I been the finder-out of this secret, it would not have relished among my other discredits. Shak.
retailer: One who retails anything; as, a retailer of merchandise; a retailer of gossip.
revibrate: To vibrate back or in return. -- Re`vi*bra"tion, n.
resumption: 1. The act of resuming; as, the resumption of a grant, of delegated powers, of an argument, of specie payments, etc. 2. (Eng.Law) The taking again into the king's hands of such lands or tenements as he had granted to any man on false suggestions or other error.
repair: 1. To return. (old) I thought . . . that he repaire should again. Chaucer. 2. To go; to betake one's self; to resort; ass, to repair to sanctuary for safety. Chaucer. | 1. The act of repairing or resorting to a place. Chaucer. The king sent a proclamation for their repair to their houses. Clarendon. 2. Place to which one repairs; a haunt; a resort.
resistible: Capable of being resisted; as, a resistible force. Sir M. Hale. -- Re*sist"i*ble*ness, n. -- Re*sist"i*bly, adv.
repetitionary: Of the nature of, or containing, repetition.
relationship: The state of being related by kindred, affinity, or other alliance. Mason.
refar: To go over again; to repeat. (old) To him therefore this wonder done refar. Fairfax.
redroot: A name of several plants having red roots, as the New Jersey tea (see under Tea), the gromwell, the bloodroot, and the Lachnanthes tinctoria, an endogenous plant found in sandy swamps from Rhode Island to Florida.
reviviscency: The act of reviving, or the state of being revived; renewal of life. In this age we have a sort of reviviscence, not, I fear, of the power, but of a taste for the power, of the early times. Coleridge.
resettle: To settle again, or a second time.
resentingly: 1. With deep sense or strong perception. (old) Dr. H. More. 2. With a sense of wrong or affront; with resentment.
republic: 1. Common weal. (old) B. Jonson. 2. A state in which the sovereign power resides in the whole body of the people, and is exercised by representatives elected by them; a commonwealth. Cf. Democracy, 2.
recognizee: The person in whose favor a recognizance is made. [Written also recognisee.] Blackstone.
recidivism: The state or quality of being recidivous; relapse, specif. (Criminology), a falling back or relapse into prior criminal habits, esp. after conviction and punishment. The old English system of recognizances, in which the guilty party deposits a sum of money, is an excellent guarantee to society against recidivism. Havelock Ellis.
reflorescence: A blossoming anew of a plant after it has apparently ceased blossoming for the season.
reproof: 1. Refutation; confutation; contradiction. (old) 2. An expression of blame or censure; especially, blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; chiding; reproach. Those best can bear reproof who merit praise. Pope. Syn. -- Admonition; reprehension; chiding; reprimand; rebuke; censure; blame. See Admonition.
retromingency: The quality or state of being retromingent. Sir T. Browne.
remean: To give meaning to; to explain the meaning of; to interpret. (old) Wyclif.
redressment: The act of redressing; redress. Jefferson.
recalcitrate: To kick against; to show repugnance to; to rebuff. The more heartily did one disdain his disdain, and recalcitrate his tricks. De Quincey. | To kick back; to kick against anything; hence, to express repugnance or opposition.
remiss: Not energetic or exact in duty or business; not careful or prompt in fulfilling engagements; negligent; careless; tardy; behindhand; lagging; slack; hence, lacking earnestness or activity; languid; | The act of being remiss; inefficiency; failure. (old) "Remisses of laws." Puttenham.
regnant: 1. Exercising regal authority; reigning; as, a queen regnant. 2. Having the chief power; ruling; predominant; prevalent. "A traitor to the vices regnant." Swift.
respection: The act of respecting; respect; regard. (old) Without difference or respection of persons. Tyndale.
reapplication: The act of reapplying, or the state of being reapplied.
repatriate: To restore to one's own country.
revealer: One who, or that which, reveals.
rennet: A name of many different kinds of apples. Cf. Reinette. Mortimer. | The inner, or mucous, membrance of the fourth stomach of the calf, or other young ruminant; also, an infusion or preparation of it, used for coagulating milk. [Written also runnet.] Cheese rennet.
real: A small Spanish silver coin; also, a denomination of money of account, formerly the unit of the Spanish monetary system. Note: A real of plate (coin) varied in value according to the time of its… | Royal; regal; kingly. (old) "The blood real of Thebes." Chaucer.
restrainable: Capable of being restrained; controllable. Sir T. Browne.
reluct: To strive or struggle against anything; to make resistance; to draw back; to feel or show repugnance or reluctance. Apt to reluct at the excesses of it [passion]. Walton.
reproducer: One who, or that which, reproduces. Burke.
reprover: One who, or that which, reproves.
reputedly: In common opinion or estimation; by repute.
reparation: 1. The act of renewing, restoring, etc., or the state of being renewed or repaired; as, the reparation of a bridge or of a highway; -- in this sense, repair is oftener used. Arbuthnot. 2. The act of making amends or giving satisfaction or compensation for a wrong, injury, etc.; also, the thing done or given; amends; satisfaction; indemnity. make reparation or reparations.
refer: 1. To carry or send back. (old) Chaucer. 2. Hence: To send or direct away; to send or direct elsewhere, as for treatment, aid, infirmation, decision, etc.; to make over, or pass over, to another; | 1. To have recourse; to apply; to appeal; to betake one's self; as, to refer to a dictionary. In suits . . . it is to refer to some friend of trust. Bacon. 2. To have relation or reference;
recursion: The act of recurring; return. (old) Boyle.
restriction: 1. The act of restricting, or state of being restricted; confinement within limits or bounds. This is to have the same restriction with all other recreations,that it be made a divertisement. Giv. of Tonque. 2. That which restricts; limitation; restraint; as, restrictions on trade.
revolutionism: The state of being in revolution; revolutionary doctrines or principles.
reconcentration: The act of reconcentrating or the state of being reconcentrated; esp., the act or policy of concentrating the rural population in or about towns and villages for convenience in political or military administration, as in Cuba during the revolution of 1895-98.
resilience: 1. The act of resiling, springing back, or rebounding; as, the resilience of a ball or of sound. 2. (Mech. & Engyn.) The mechanical work required to strain an elastic body, as a deflected beam, stretched spring, etc., to the elastic limit; also, the work performed by the body in recovering from such strain.
reparable: Capable of being repaired, restored to a sound or good state, or made good; restorable; as, a reparable injury.
repugnable: Capable of being repugned or resisted. Sir T. North.
retiform: Composed of crossing lines and interstices; reticular; netlike; as, the retiform coat of the eye.
refulgence: The quality of being refulgent; brilliancy; splender; radiance.
redsear: To be brittle when red-hot; to be red-short. Moxon.
restorable: Admitting of being restored; capable of being reclaimed; as, restorable land. Swift. -- Re*stor"a*ble*ness, n.
rehearse: 1. To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite. Chaucer. When the words were heard which David spake, they rehearsed them before Saul. 1 Sam. xvii. 31. 2. To narrate; | To recite or repeat something for practice. "There will we rehearse." Shak.
redintegrate: Restored to wholeness or a perfect state; renewed. Bacon. | To make whole again; a renew; to restore to integrity or soundness. The English nation seems obliterated. What could redintegrate us again Coleridge.
requirement: 1. The act of requiring; demand; requisition. 2. That which is required; an imperative or authoritative command; an essential condition; something needed or necessary; a need. One of those who believe that they can fill up every requirement contained in the rule of righteousness. J. M. Mason.
resenter: One who resents. Sir H. Wotton.
retired: 1. Private; secluded; quiet; as, a retired life; a person of retired habits. A retired part of the peninsula. Hawthorne. 2. Withdrawn from active duty or business; as, a retired officer; a retired physician. Retired flank (Fort.), a flank bent inward toward the rear of the work. -- Retired list (Mil.
remorse: 1. The anguish, like gnawing pain, excited by a sense of guilt; compunction of conscience for a crime committed, or for the sins of one's past life. "Nero will be tainted with remorse." Shak. 2. Sympathetic sorrow; pity; compassion. Curse on the unpardoning prince, whom tears can draw To no remorse. Dryden.
reprobation: 1. The act of reprobating; the state of being reprobated; strong disapproval or censure. The profligate pretenses upon which he was perpetually soliciting an increase of his disgraceful stipend are mentioned with becoming reprobation. Jeffrey. Set a brand of reprobation on clipped poetry and false coin. Dryden. 2.
repellence: The principle of repulsion; the quality or capacity of repelling; repulsion.
redact: To reduce to form, as literary matter; to digest and put in shape (matter for publication); to edit.
repaganize: To paganize anew; to bring back to paganism.
reviction: Return to life. (old) Sir T. Browne.
rehibitory: Of or relating to rehibition; as, a rehibitory action.
rescription: A writing back; the answering of a letter. Loveday.
retrace: 1. To trace back, as a line. Then if the line of Turnus you retrace, He springs from Inachus of Argive race. Driden. 2. To go back, in or over (a previous course); to go over again in a reverse direction; as, to retrace one's steps; to retrace one's proceedings. 3. To trace over again, or renew the outline of, as a drawing; to draw again.
requital: The act of requiting; also, that which requites; return, good or bad, for anything done; in a good sense, compensation; recompense; as, the requital of services; in a bad sense, retaliation, or punishment; as, the requital of evil deeds. No merit their aversion can remove, Nor ill requital can efface their love. Waller. Syn. -- Compensation; recompense; remuneration; reward;
reboation: Repetition of a bellow. Bp. Patrick.
regrowth: The act of regrowing; a second or new growth. Darwin. The regrowth of limbs which had been cut off. A. B. Buckley.
revengement: Revenge. (old) He 'll breed revengement and a scourge for me. Shak.
refugee: 1. One who flees to a shelter, or place of safety. 2. Especially, one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign power or country for safety; as, the French refugees who left France after the revocation of the edict of Nantes.
reclusion: A state of retirement from the world; seclusion.
reliquidate: To liquidate anew; to adjust a second time.
revulse: To pull back with force. Cowper.
reichsrath: The parliament of Austria (exclusive of Hungary, which has its own diet, or parliament). It consists of an Upper and a Lower House, or a House of Lords and a House of Representatives.
reascension: The act of reascending; a remounting.
recent: 1. Of late origin, existence, or occurrence; lately come; not of remote date, antiquated style, or the like; not already known, familiar, worn out, trite, etc.; fresh; novel; new; modern; as, recent news. The ancients were of opinion, that a considerable portion of that country [Egypt] was recent, and formed out of the mud discharged into the neighboring sea by the Nile.
reed: The fourth stomach of a ruminant; rennet. [Prov. Eng. or Scot.] | 1. (Bot.) A name given to many tall and coarse grasses or grasslike plants, and their slender, often jointed, stems, such as the various kinds of bamboo, and especially the common reed of Europe and…
retiring: 1. Reserved; shy; not forward or obtrusive; as, retiring modesty; retiring manners. 2. Of or pertaining to retirement; causing retirement; suited to, or belonging to, retirement. Retiring board (Mil.), a board of officers who consider and report upon the alleged incapacity of an officer for active service.
revoke: 1. To call or bring back; to recall. (old) The faint sprite he did revoke again, To her frail mansion of morality. Spenser. 2. Hence, to annul, by recalling or taking back; to repeal; to rescind; | To fail to follow suit when holding a card of the suit led, in violation of the rule of the game; to renege. Hoyle.
reducer: One who, or that which, reduces.
revivalism: The spirit of religious revivals; the methods of revivalists.
renvoy: To send back. (old) "Not dismissing or renvoying her." Bacon.
remonstrative: Having the character of a remonstrance; expressing remonstrance.
repel: 1. To drive back; to force to return; to check the advance of; to repulse as, to repel an enemy or an assailant. Hippomedon repelled the hostile tide. Pope. They repelled each other strongly, and yet… | To act with force in opposition to force impressed; to exercise repulsion.
recognizer: One who recognizes; a recognizor. [Written also recogniser.]
republicate: To make public again; to republish. (old)
readjust: To adjust or settle again; to put in a different order or relation; to rearrange.
remittitur: (a) A remission or surrender, -- remittitur damnut being a remission of excess of damages. (b) A sending back, as when a record is remitted by a superior to an inferior court. Wharton.
rettery: A place or establishment where flax is retted. See Ret. Ure.
rensselaerite: A soft, compact variety of talc,, being an altered pyroxene. It is often worked in a lathe into inkstands and other articles.
restive: Unwilling to go on; obstinate in refusing to move forward; stubborn; drawing back. Restive or resty, drawing back, instead of going forward, as some horses do. E. Philips (1658). The people remarked with awe and wonder that the beasts which were to drag him [Abraham Holmes] to the gallows became restive, and went back. Macaulay. 2. Inactive; sluggish. (old) Sir T. Browne. 3.
rentable: Capable of being rented, or suitable for renting.
remittee: One to whom a remittance is sent.
respond: 1. To say somethin in return; to answer; to reply; as, to respond to a question or an argument. 2. To show some effect in return to a force; to act in response; to accord; to correspond; to suit. | 1. To answer; to reply. 2. To suit or accord with; to correspond to. For his great deeds respond his speeches great. Fairfax.
repugn: To fight against; to oppose; to resist. Stubbornly he did repugn the truth. Shak.
reelection: Election a second time, or anew; as, the reëlection of a former chief.
restrainer: One who, or that which, restrains.
recessional: Of or pertaining to recession or withdrawal. Recessional hymn, a hymn sung in a procession returning from the choir to the robing room.
recreant: 1. Crying for mercy, as a combatant in the trial by battle; yielding; cowardly; mean-spirited; craven. "This recreant knight." Spenser. 2. Apostate; false; unfaithful. | One who yields in combat, and begs for mercy; a mean-spirited, cowardly wretch. Blackstone. You are all recreants and dastards! Shak.
recriminatory: Having the quality of recrimination; retorting accusation; recriminating.
retina: The delicate membrane by which the back part of the globe of the eye is lined, and in which the fibers of the optic nerve terminate. See Eye. Note: The fibers of the optic nerve and the retinal blood vessels spread out upon the front surface of the retina, while the sensory layer (called Jacob's membrane), containing the rods and cones, is on the back side, next the choroid…
receivable: Capable of being received. -- Re*ceiv"a*ble*ness, n. Bills receivable. See under 6th Bill.
realistic: Of or pertaining to the realists; in the manner of the realists; characterized by realism rather than by imagination.
reeden: Consisting of a reed or reeds. Through reeden pipes convey the golden flood. Dryden.
resting: a. & n. from Rest, v. t. & i. Resting spore (Bot.), a spore in certain orders of algæ, which remains quiescent, retaining its vitality, for long periods of time. C. E. Bessey.
repudiable: Admitting of repudiation; fit or proper to be put away.
regatta: Originally, a gondola race in Venice; now, a rowing or sailing race, or a series of such races.
respiratory: Of or pertaining to respiration; serving for respiration; as, the respiratory organs; respiratory nerves; the respiratory function; respiratory changes. Respiratory foods. (Physiol.) See 2d Note under Food, n., 1. -- Respiratory tree (Zoöl.), the branched internal gill of certain holothurians.
restrict: To restrain within bounds; to limit; to confine; as, to restrict worlds to a particular meaning; to restrict a patient to a certain diet. Syn. -- To limit; bound; circumscribe; restrain; repress; curb; coerce.
reordain: To ordain again, as when the first ordination is considered defective. Bp. Burnet.
retrench: 1. To cut off; to pare away. Thy exuberant parts retrench. Denham. 2. To lessen; to abridge; to curtail; as, to retrench superfluities or expenses. But this thy glory shall be soon retrenched. | To cause or suffer retrenchment; specifically, to cut down living expenses; as, it is more reputable to retrench than to live embarrassed.
reforge: To forge again or anew; hence, to fashion or fabricate anew; to make over. Udall.
response: 1. The act of responding. 2. An answer or reply. Specifically: (a) Reply to an objection in formal disputation. I. Watts. (b) (Eccl.) The answer of the people or congregation to the priest or clergyman, in the litany and other parts of divine service. (c) (R.C.Ch.) A kind of anthem sung after the lessons of matins and some other parts of the office.
reanimation: The act or operation of reanimating, or the state of being reanimated; reinvigoration; revival.
remembrance: 1. The act of remembering; a holding in mind, or bringing to mind; recollection. Lest fierce remembrance wake my sudden rage. Milton. Lest the remembrance of his grief should fail. Addison. 2. The state of being remembered, or held in mind; memory; recollection. This, ever grateful, in remembrance bear. Pope. 3. Something remembered; a person or thing kept in memory. Shak. 4.
releaser: One who releases, or sets free.
reinforce: See Reënforce, v. t. | See Reënforce, n.
restorative: Of or pertaining to restoration; having power to restore. Destroys life's enemy, Hunger, with sweet restorative delight. Milton. | Something which serves to restore; especially, a restorative medicine. Arbuthnot.
restorer: One who, or that which, restores.
realization: The act of realizing, or the state of being realized.
regain: To gain anew; to get again; to recover, as what has escaped or been lost; to reach again. Syn. -- To recover; reobtain; repossess; retrieve.
remediless: 1. Not admitting of a remedy; incapable of being restored or corrected; incurable; irreparable; as, a remediless mistake or loss. "Chains remedilesse." Spenser. Hopeless are all my evils, all remediless. Milton. 2. Not answering as a remedy; ineffectual. (old) Forced to forego the attempt remediless. Spenser. Syn. -- Incurable; cureless; irremediable; irrecoverable;
renderer: 1. One who renders. 2. A vessel in which lard or tallow, etc., is rendered.
recension: 1. The act of reviewing or revising; review; examination; enumeration. Barrow. 2. Specifically, the review of a text (as of an ancient author) by an editor; critical revisal and establishment. 3. The result of such a work; a text established by critical revision; an edited version.
retroactive: Fitted or designed to retroact; operating by returned action; affecting what is past; retrospective. Beddoes. Retroactive law or statute (Law), one which operates to make criminal or punishable, or in any way expressly to affect, acts done prior to the passing of the law.
retrovaccination: The inoculation of a cow with human vaccine virus.
refractiveness: The quality or condition of being refractive.
recumbent: Leaning; reclining; lying; as, the recumbent posture of the Romans at their meals. Hence, figuratively; Resting; inactive; idle. -- Re*cum"bent*ly, adv.
request: 1. The act of asking for anything desired; expression of desire or demand; solicitation; prayer; petition; entreaty. I will marry her, sir, at your request. Shak. 2. | 1. To ask for (something); to express desire ffor; to solicit; as, to request his presence, or a favor. 2. To address with a request; to ask. I request you To give my poor host freedom. Shak. Syn.
ream: Cream; also, the cream or froth on ale. [Scot.] | To cream; to mantle. [Scot.] A huge pewter measuring pot which, in the language of the hostess, reamed with excellent claret. Sir W. Scott.
reargument: An arguing over again, as of a motion made in court.
recognizability: The quality or condition of being recognizable.
repetend: That part of a circulating decimal which recurs continually, ad infinitum: -- sometimes indicated by a dot over the first and last repetend is 283.
retchless: Careless; reckless. (old) Dryden. --- Retch"less*ly, adv. -- Retch"less*ness, n. (old)
redly: In a red manner; with redness.
reveille: The beat of drum, or bugle blast, about break of day, to give notice that it is time for the soldiers to rise, and for the sentinels to forbear challenging. "Sound a reveille." Dryden. For at dawning to assail ye Here no bugles sound reveille. Sir W. Scott.
rejectaneous: Not chosen orr received; rejected. (old) "Profane, rejectaneous, and reprobate people." Barrow.
restorationism: The belief or doctrines of the Restorationists.
recusant: Obstinate in refusal; specifically, in English history, refusing to acknowledge the supremacy of the king in the churc, or to conform to the established rites of the church; as, a recusant lord. | 1. One who is obstinate in refusal; one standing out stubbornly against general practice or opinion. The last rebellious recusants among the European family of nations. De Quincey. 2. (Eng.
reedification: The act reëdifying; the state of being reëdified.
resplendent: Shining with brilliant luster; very bright. -- Re*splen"dent*ly, adv. With royal arras and resplendent gold. Spenser.
refuter: One who, or that which, refutes.
recrudescent: 1. Growing raw, sore, or painful again. 2. Breaking out again after temporary abatement or supression; as, a recrudescent epidemic.
repopulation: The act of repeopling; act of furnishing with a population anew.
repedation: A stepping or going back. (old) Dr. H. More.
relation: 1. The act of relating or telling; also, that which is related; recital; account; narration; narrative; as, the relation of historical events. relation doth well figure them. Bacon. 2. The state of being related or of referring; what is apprehended as appertaining to a being or quality, by considering it in its bearing upon something else; relative quality or condition;
reserved: 1. Kept for future or special use, or for an exigency; as, reserved troops; a reserved seat in a theater. 2. Restrained from freedom in words or actions; backward, or cautious, in communicating one's thoughts and feelings; not free or frank. To all obliging, yet reserved to all. Walsh. Nothing reserved or sullen was to see. Dryden. -- Re*serv"ed*ly (r, adv.
rectinerved: Having the veins or nerves straight; -- said of leaves.
reflex: 1. Directed back; attended by reflection; retroactive; introspective. The reflex act of the soul, or the turning of the intellectual eye inward upon its own actions. Sir M. Hale. 2. | 1. Reflection; the light reflected from an illuminated surface to one in shade. Yon gray is not the morning's eye, 'Tis but the pale reflex of Cynthia's brow. Shak.
reclusely: In a recluse or solitary manner.
repulsion: 1. The act of repulsing or repelling, or the state of being repulsed or repelled. 2. A feeling of violent offence or disgust; repugnance. 3. (Physics) The power, either inherent or due to some physical action, by which bodies, or the particles of bodies, are made to recede from each other, or to resist each other's nearer approach; as, molecular repulsion; electrical repulsion.
redargue: To disprove; to refute; toconfute; to reprove; to convict. (old) How shall I . . . suffer that God should redargue me at doomsday, and the angels reproach my lukewarmness Jer. Taylor. Now this objection to the immediate cognition of external objects has, as far as I know, been redargued in three different ways. Sir W. Hamilton.
regardable: Worthy of regard or notice; to be regarded; observable. Sir T. Browne.
resale: A sale at second hand, or at retail; also, a second sale. Bacon.
reservatory: A place in which things are reserved or kept. Woodward.
repulsive: 1. Serving, or able, to repulse; repellent; as, a repulsive force. Repulsive of his might the weapon stood. Pope. 2. Cold; forbidding; offensive; as, repulsive manners. -- Re*pul"sive*ly, adv. -- Re*pul"sive*ness, n.
registrar: One who registers; a recorder; a keeper of records; as, a registrar of births, deaths, and marriages. See Register, n., 3.
repealer: One who repeals; one who seeks a repeal; specifically, an advocate for the repeal of the Articles of Union between Great Britain and Ireland.
reprehend: To reprove or reprimand with a view of restraining, checking, or preventing; to make charge of fault against; to disapprove of; to chide; to blame; to censure. Chaucer. Aristippus being reprehended of luxury by one that was not rich, for that he gave six crowns for a small fish. Bacon. Pardon me for reprehending thee. Shak. In which satire human vices, ignorance, and errors .
repayable: Capable of being, or proper to be , repaid; due; as, a loan repayable in ten days; services repayable in kind.
rememorate: To recall something by means of memory; to remember. (old) Bryskett.
reimpregnate: To impregnate again or anew. Sir T. Browne.
rei: A portuguese money of account, in value about one tenth of a cent. [Spelt also ree.]
remain: 1. To stay behind while others withdraw; to be left after others have been removed or destroyed; to be left after a number or quantity has been subtracted or cut off; | To await; to be left to. (old) The easier conquest now remains thee. Milton.
reconvertible: Capable of being reconverted; convertible again to the original form or condition.
resource: 1. That to which one resorts orr on which one depends for supply or support; means of overcoming a difficulty; resort; expedient. Threat'nings mixed with prayers, his last resource. Dryden. 2. pl. Pecuniary means; funds; money, or any property that can be converted into supplies; available means or capabilities of any kind.
realize: 1. To make real; to convert from the imaginary or fictitious into the actual; to bring into concrete existence; to accomplish; as, to realize a scheme or project. | To convert any kind of property into money, especially property representing investments, as shares in stock companies, bonds, etc. Wary men took the alarm, and began to realize, a word now first…
remittal: A remitting; a giving up; surrender; as, the remittal of the first fruits. Swift.
reasonably: 1. In a reasonable manner. 2. Moderately; tolerably. "Reasonably perfect in the language." Holder.
resupinate: Inverted in position; appearing to be upside down or reversed, as the flowers of the orchis and the leaves of some plants.
regurgitate: To throw or pour back, as from a deep or hollow place; to pour or throw back in great quantity. | To be thrown or poured back; to rush or surge back. The food may regurgitatem the stomach into the esophagus and mouth. Quain.
regnancy: The condition or quality of being regnant; sovereignty; rule. Coleridge.
refossion: The act of digging up again. (old) Bp. Hall.
repass: To pass again; to pass or travel over in the opposite direction; to pass a second time; as, to repass a bridge or a river; to repass the sea. | To pass or go back; to move back; as, troops passing and repassing before our eyes.
remorseless: Being without remorse; having no pity; hence, destitute of sensibility; cruel; insensible to distress; merciless. "Remorseless adversaries." South. "With remorseless cruelty." Milton. Syn. -- Unpitying; pitiless; relentless; unrelenting; implacable; merciless; unmerciful; savage; cruel. -- Re*morse"less*ly, adv. -- Re*morse"less*ness, n.
recruitment: The act or process of recruiting; especially, the enlistment of men for an army.
repay: 1. To pay back; to refund; as, to repay money borrowed or advanced. If you repay me not on such a day, In such a place, such sum or sums. Shak. 2. To make return or requital for; to recompense; -- in a good or bad sense; as, to repay kindness; to repay an injury. Benefits which can not be repaid . . . are not commonly found to increase affection. Rambler. 3.
renverse: To reverse. (old) Whose shield he bears renverst. Spenser. | Reversed; set with the head downward; turned contrary to the natural position.
reconsideration: The act of reconsidering, or the state of being reconsidered; as, the reconsideration of a vote in a legislative body.
religious: 1. redingote: A long plain double-breasted outside coat for women.
restharrow: A European leguminous plant (Ononis arvensis) with long, tough roots.

retrospection: The act, or the faculty, of looking back on things past.
rectoress: 1. A governess; a rectrix. Drayton. 2. The wife of a rector. Thackeray.
respersion: The act of sprinkling or scattering. (old)
replantation: The act of planting again; a replanting. Hallywell.
repartimiento: A partition or distribution, especially of slaves; also, an assessment of taxes. W. Irving.
reseau: (a) (Astron.) A system of lines forming small squares of standard size, which is photographed, by a separate exposure, on the same plate with star images to facilitate measurements, detect changes of the film, etc. (b) In lace, a ground or foundation of regular meshes, like network.
reviviscent: Able or disposed to revive; reviving. E. Darwin.

rectorate: The office, rank, or station of a rector; rectorship.

reimpression: A second or repeated impression; a reprint.
recoveror: The demandant in a common recovery after judgment. Wharton.

reliability: The state or quality of being reliable; reliableness.
